correctness.rationale: The proof fixes the exact denominator convention and all quantifiers. Encoding distinct squarefree semiprimes as edges of a simple prime graph is exact. After multiplication by the product of all support primes, reduction modulo any vertex q different from p proves that q cannot have degree one. This rules out one and two terms and forces every three-edge representation to be a triangle on p,q,r. The triangle identity is algebraically equivalent to \(\(\((q-1)(r-1)=p+1\)\)\), and the converse is immediate. The p congruent to 1 modulo 4 corollary follows because two odd shifted primes would make the product divisible by four. Finiteness of the minimum uses Li's theorem for squarefree denominators. Finite computation is explicitly not used as proof.

broader_coverage.reasoning: Li's September theorem is broader in target coverage but existential: it supplies some finite representation for every squarefree denominator and does not bound or classify the minimum length. The June paper does not reach all small rational targets. Butler--Erdos--Graham use three-prime denominators, so their theorem is on a different denominator class.

The earlier semiprime paper treats natural numbers and above-threshold rationals, also without this short-support result. Exact published-findings database and web searches for the triangle identity, shifted-prime factorization, minimum length, and graph-leaf obstruction found no publication stating the theorem. The nearest database findings concern different Egyptian-fraction-like or prime-support objects and do not imply the claim.

value.rationale: This is a natural complete classification of the first possible representation length in a denominator-restricted Egyptian-fraction problem solved only days earlier. Prime denominators are the simplest squarefree denominators that are not themselves allowable semiprimes, and the source theorem guarantees their representability without addressing length. The result turns the three-term layer into an exact shifted-prime factorization problem and, for p congruent to 1 modulo 4, identifies it exactly with the twin-prime condition. This is structural information rather than a routine recomputation or arbitrary finite slice.
